events.title: The year 2000 brings limited computer disruption
events.description: After years of preparation, the date change causes fewer problems than many people feared. Some errors still need fixing.

events.title: Technology shares reach a peak
events.description: The Nasdaq stock index closes at a high on March 10. It is only later that people can identify this as the peak.

events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Thousands of people are killed. US stock markets close for four trading days and reopen on September 17.

events.title: Economists announce a recession
events.description: Researchers say the long period of economic growth ended in March 2001. Their announcement comes in November.

events.title: The Fed starts raising interest rates
events.description: The Federal Reserve raises its target for short-term interest rates from 1% to 1.25% as the economy grows.

what_happened_next.text:
All three featured shares finished below their September 1999 starting values: Microsoft at about 62 cents per dollar, Cisco at 53 cents and Amazon at 51 cents. A mix of U.S. or international shares ended near where it began, while cash grew a little and government bonds grew more. A growing technology industry did not protect every company share from a fall.

The companies’ business news was mixed. Microsoft reported more than 67 million Windows XP licenses sold by 2002. Cisco’s 2001 results included a $2.2 billion inventory charge and a large loss as equipment sales slowed. Amazon’s 2003 sales rose 34%, and it reported a small annual profit after a loss in 2002. Better sales or a new product do not automatically translate into a higher share price.

The Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 before falling for several years. The U.S. economy entered a recession from March to November 2001, and the September 11 attacks caused terrible loss of life while markets were unsettled. The Y2K date change brought fewer computer disruptions than many feared after years of preparation. People in September 1999 could not know how these five years would unfold.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: People followed software rivalries, new internet businesses, the coming year 2000, troubles in other countries, storms, sports, and entertainment.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The stock market fell, and the economy moved into and then out of a recession. Choosing one company instead of a basket of many companies could lead to very different results.
reflection.what_faded_away: Many people worried that computers would fail when calendars changed to 2000. After years of preparation, the new year came with little disruption. Product stories and sports soon made way for other news.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: In September 1999, no one knew when technology stocks would fall, how long the slide would last, or when the economy would go into recession. No one could know the September 11 attacks were coming. Popular companies did not make the future certain.

hot:1999-09:microsoft.text: By October 2002, Microsoft said more than 67 million Windows XP licenses had sold since its October 2001 launch. Yet $1 invested in Microsoft in September 1999 ended near 62 cents five years later: strong software demand did not keep its shares from falling during this window.

hot:1999-09:cisco.text: On May 8, 2001, Cisco reported quarterly sales of $4.73 billion, down 4% from a year earlier. It recorded a $2.2 billion charge for excess inventory and a $2.69 billion net loss as orders for networking equipment slowed sharply.

hot:1999-09:amazon.text: Amazon’s sales rose 34% to $5.26 billion in 2003, and it reported $35 million in net income after a $149 million loss in 2002. Lower prices and a wider product selection helped attract shoppers while the company moved toward more profitable operations. Yet $1 invested in September 1999 ended near 51 cents five years later.
